top_choice_rationale: P003 (Autor, Dorn, Hanson) offers the most checkable and best-scrutinised evidence on the list. Its core design, local labour-market exposure to import competition, is transparent and has been re-run and criticised for a decade or more. On my recollection, which I have not verified, the qualitative findings of slow adjustment and lasting local costs have survived that scrutiny, while the aggregate magnitude remains debated. The citation should therefore name identified evidence on local adjustment and avoid claiming a number or the whole task framework. The three-person unit is the natural co-authored core of that evidence, and Dorn is the right third name over Katz. The costs are real: task-theory credit sits partly with Levy, Murnane, Acemoglu and Restrepo, Katz is excluded, and recent labour prizes are adjacent. I rank P002 second because its credit line is the most defensible three-person cut within B014 if the citation is confined to nominal-rigidity theory and policy rules, though the eight-name pool and model-dependent empirics weigh against it. P001 is third: its credit line is cleaner but its welfare claims are more assumption-dependent. P004 is fourth, because of the observational identification and the partial overlap with the 2024 prize. Any of these would be preferable to no award.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile. None of the credited names appears among my documented co-authors or collaborators. My replication and many-analyst interests shape how I weigh scrutiny of designs, a lens I applied to all candidates. Disclosed, not adjudicated.
